# Robust Multi-step Model Predictive Control with Feasibility Guarantees 

Sebastian Steffen 

sebastian.steffen@eng.ox.ac.uk 

Mark Cannon 

mark.cannon@eng.ox.ac.uk 

Abstract —We present a method of ensuring recursive feasibil-ity and stability for robust nonlinear Model Predictive Control (MPC) with multi-step predictors. Although feasibility guarantees are well-established for the case of single-step models applied recursively over a finite horizon, such guarantees are missing in naive MPC formulations that use distinct multi-step models to predict the system state at different future points in time. This issue arises because of potential inconsistencies in multi-step predictions generated at different times. Our approach checks for possible infeasibility of the robust nonlinear MPC optimisation problem a priori , and uses information from previous solutions to provide a fall-back based on previously verified reachable sets. We illustrate the proposed predictor-substitution strategy with a simple numerical example. 

I. I NTRODUCTION 

Model Predictive Control (MPC) is a widely used control strategy based on optimising the predicted future behaviour of a system. MPC is applicable to problems with state and input constraints, external disturbances and model uncertainty [1], [2]. At each discrete time-step, a constrained receding horizon optimal control problem (RHOCP) is solved to find the control sequence that minimises a performance criterion over a future horizon. Nonlinear MPC has found applications across arange of industrial processes and engineering systems due to the potential for nonlinear models to accurately predict system evolution [3], [1]. Nonlinear models present additional challenges over linear MPC however, including increased online computational load since the RHOCP is in general a nonconvex nonlinear program (NLP), and the need for more sophisticated tools to ensure robustness by propagating the effects of disturbances and model uncertainty through nonlinear dynamics. A large body of work has investigated various ways to address these issues. A common approach reformulates the optimal control problem as a sequential convex program (SCP), with the NLP typically approximated using local lin-earisations around candidate trajectories [4]. The convexified problem (often a QP) is then iterated by linearising using trajectories generated using previous solutions [5], [6]. These approaches require a method of propagating model uncertainty and approximation errors across subsequent time-steps in the prediction horizon. In our recent work [7], we propose a nonlinear MPC scheme using learnt multi-step predictors. The use of distinct functions for each of the predicted steps allows

for a simpler formulation of the SCP, which only needs to account for linearisation errors at individual future time-steps rather than bounding their accumulation over a horizon. An additional advantage of multi-step models emerges when they are derived from data rather than analytically. For the linear case, recent comparisons of single-step and multi-step models show that when models are misspecified due to partial observability, learnt multi-step models show lower compound-ing error [8], and better data-efficiency during learning [9]. In our previous work, we found that multi-step predictions using deep neural networks provided lower mean average error than recursive application of a single-step model [7]. The use of linear multi-step predictors in MPC is well-established. In [10], the authors propose a linear multi-rate MPC scheme using an autoregressive model with exogenous input (ARX) structure. The approach partitions the predic-tion horizon into blocks corresponding to multi-rate models, and in contrast to standard receding-horizon MPC, an entire block of inputs is applied before re-computation. In [11], this multi-rate approach is extended to state-space models with parametric uncertainty and combined with homothetic tubes to ensure robust constraint satisfaction. Multi-step models are identified from data in [12] and used in stochastic MPC with chance constraints. Likewise [13] considers stochastic MPC, 

> arXiv:2606.25684v1 [math.OC] 24 Jun 2026 2

but employs a probabilistic multi-step identification method which implicitly incorporates state estimation. The authors demonstrate applicability of the approach to certain nonlinear systems treating the effects of nonlinearity as disturbances. A smaller body of work has directly considered the non-linear case. In [14], kernel-based methods are used to learn multi-step nonlinear mappings from data. The authors formu-late a finite-horizon MPC problem with deterministic safety guarantees, and propose a method for using information from previous solutions to tighten predicted uncertainty sets and reduce conservatism. However, to the best of our knowledge, no nonlinear MPC schemes with multi-step predictors are able to ensure recursive feasibility of the optimal control problem. Moreover, existing multi-step linear MPC schemes with recur-sive feasibility guarantees rely on multi-rate formulations, and therefore do not use the standard receding-horizon approach of recomputing the control sequence at each sampling step, given the latest state or output measurement. We present a novel approach for guaranteeing feasibility with multi-step predictors, given the existence of an initial solution to the RHOCP. Each time the RHOCP is solved on-line, the method first identifies a suboptimal feasible solution by searching over a set of candidate trajectories, replacing predictions that violate constraints with previously verified alternatives via a predictor substitution strategy (Fig. 1). Robustness to possible infeasibility of a terminal condition is ensured through a variable horizon strategy. Our method applies to general nonlinear multi-step prediction models with bounded additive disturbances. The paper is organised as follows. After the problem formu-lation in Section II, Sections III and IV discuss tube MPC with single-step and multi-step models and explain the proposed predictor substitution algorithm. Section V gives the RHOCP for multi-step MPC with feasibility and stability guarantees. A numerical example demonstrating the application of the algo-rithm is discussed in Section VI, and we provide concluding remarks in Section VII. II. P ROBLEM FORMULATION

A. Checking constraint satisfaction a priori 

A computationally inexpensive sufficient condition for RHOCP feasibility can be checked by evaluating the state and input trajectories generated by a prescribed set of control-perturbation sequences. Let Vk be a set of candidate pertur-bation sequences at time k, and let I(x, v 0: N −1, N ) denote, for given v0: N −1, initial state x, and horizon N , the indices of prediction time-steps at which state or control constraints are violated by the multi-step prediction models of (5): 

I(x, v 0: N −1, N ) = {i ∈ { 1, . . . , N } : Xi(x, v 0: i−1) ⊈ X ,

or κ(Xi(x, v 0: i−1)) ⊕ { vi} ⊈ U , (17) or XN (x, v 0: N −1) ⊈ X T }.

A sufficient condition for RHOCP feasibility at time k is 

∃ v0: N −1|k ∈ Vk such that I(xk, v 0: N −1|k, N ) = ∅. (18) Given a candidate perturbation set Vk, this is the basis of a method for ensuring a priori that the RHOCP is feasible. 

B. Feasibility recovery and predictor substitution

This set must contain ˜v0: N −1|k defined in (13), but it may also contain other sequences that are likely to yield a feasible prob-lem with few predictor substitutions (Appendix A-D proposes one such candidate perturbation sequence for the numerical example in Section VI). Since the predictor substitutions in S

(computed in line 10) are only guaranteed to satisfy constraints if v0: N −1 = ˜ v0: N −1|k, we perform an additional constraint check (lines 11-12). The constraint (22) on the predicted cost applies simultaneously to all stages, therefore its feasibility is checked (line 13) after computing S. If it is possible to generate a feasible problem using a candidate sequence in 5

Vk, the for loop (lines 7-16) determines the fewest predictor substitutions required and stores their indices in Imin (line 16). If no candidate in Vk generates a feasible problem, the algorithm executes the next iteration of the while loop with 

¯N reduced by 1 until ¯N = max {1, ¯Nk−1 − 1}. At this point, a feasible RHOCP is guaranteed to exist, possibly using substituted predictors at every step, in which case |I min | = ¯N

and si|k = si+1 |k−1 for i = 1 , . . . , ¯N .V. M ULTI -STEP MPC WITH PREDICTOR SUBSTITUTION

Implementation details for this example are provided in Ap-pendix A. The procedure for computing multi-step disturbance sets is given in Section A-A. The computation of the terminal set and feedback law is described in Section A-B. The methods for evaluating the infeasible index set I and computing the candidate perturbation set Vk are described in Sections A-C and A-D. Finally, a Sequential Convex Programming (SCP) approach for solving the RHOCP is discussed in Section A-E. To create a situation in which inconsistent multi-step pre-dictors result in an infeasible problem, we artificially inflate the disturbance sets for prediction time-steps i = 3 and i = 4 

by a factor of two. This leads to sufficient inconsistency in predicted tubes at successive time-steps to create a situation where, without the use of the predictor substitution algorithm, the multi-step RHOCP becomes infeasible at time-steps k = 1 

and k = 2 despite being feasible at k = 0 . However, the predictor substitution procedure of Algorithm 1 constructs feasible problems using substitutions at k = 1 and k = 2 . For all time-steps k ⩾ 3, no further substitutions are required. The controller is implemented using CVXPY [16] and CLARA-BEL [17]. Figure 3 shows the resulting predicted and closed-loop trajectories. VII. C ONCLUSIONS AND FUTURE DIRECTIONS 

This paper presents a novel method for guaranteeing re-cursive feasibility of robust receding horizon multi-step MPC. The strategy employs predictor substitutions to avoid poten-tial infeasibility of the multi-step RHOCP that arises from inconsistencies in robust predictors at different time-steps. Crucially, the proposed method does not depend on a multi-rate formulation, and therefore allows the optimal control sequence to be recomputed at each time-step, given the latest Fig. 3. Predicted state tubes and closed loop trajectories for various time-steps, showing the predicted state sets generated using substitued predictors 7

state information. The algorithm is agnostic to the specific so-lution technique for the nonlinear RHOCP. We demonstrate the functionality of the algorithm via a simple numerical example. A limitation of the approach is that predictor substitutions may introduce unnecessary suboptimality if the prediction horizon is reduced to maintain a prediction format consisting of one predictor per time-step. Future work will consider relaxing this requirement by allowing each prediction time-step to be defined by arbitrary compositions of multi-step predictors, and will investigate methods of constructing candidate control sequences for checking feasibility.
